messages.check.binding-conflict.compares: Every keymap, user command and autocmd registration against all other registrations of the same thing.
messages.check.binding-conflict.why: Of two registrations of one key or command the last one wins without a message, and which one that is depends on load order.
messages.check.consumer-require-missing.compares: What the configured consumer projects require from this tree against the modules this tree declares.
messages.check.consumer-require-missing.why: A module renamed here breaks a consumer over there, and nothing in this tree's own requires shows it.
messages.check.dead-function.compares: Every function against the calls and mentions the tree holds of it.
messages.check.dead-function.why: A function nothing calls is either public API or dead code; the three variants say how sure the map can be about which.
messages.check.dead-readme-link.compares: Every relative link in a README against the files that exist.
messages.check.dead-readme-link.why: A link that leads nowhere is the first thing a reader of the documentation hits after a file was moved or deleted.
messages.check.dead-see-target.compares: Every `@see` target against the modules and functions of the tree.
messages.check.dead-see-target.why: A `@see` is a promise that there is more to read; one that resolves to nothing sends the reader looking for it.
messages.check.doc-references-missing.compares: The functions and fields the prose under `docs/` names against what the named module really has.
messages.check.doc-references-missing.why: Prose that names a function which is gone describes an API that no longer exists; this is the drift between documentation and code the tool is for.
messages.check.example-does-not-parse.compares: The code of every `@example` against the Lua parser.
messages.check.example-does-not-parse.why: An example is the part of the documentation people copy; one that is not valid Lua fails in the reader's hands.
messages.check.feature-module-missing.compares: The `Module:` bullet of every feature description against the files and modules of the tree.
messages.check.feature-module-missing.why: The bullet is the way from a feature to its code and back; a stale one points a reader at a file that is gone.
messages.check.file-holds-many-modules.compares: The module identities one file declares against the one identity the map can give a file.
messages.check.file-holds-many-modules.why: The map attaches functions, requires and findings to a file; with several modules in one file it cannot say which of them they belong to.
messages.check.layer-violation.compares: Every require edge against the configured layer rules (which layer may reach into which).
messages.check.layer-violation.why: The layering is a decision about the architecture; a single require across it undoes the decision without anyone having made a new one.
messages.check.missing-module-tag.compares: Every source file against the `---@module` line it should open with.
messages.check.missing-module-tag.why: The module name is what every other check and every link resolves against; a file without one is in the map only as a path.
messages.check.missing-readme.compares: The directories of the tree that should have one against a `README.md` in each.
messages.check.missing-readme.why: The README is the front door of a directory, and the map links to it from the node; a missing one is a dead end for the reader who starts there.
messages.check.missing-summary.compares: Every module against the one description line under its `@module` tag.
messages.check.missing-summary.why: The summary is the text every list, box and search result shows for the module; without it the map names the file and says nothing about it.
messages.check.module-path-mismatch.compares: The name a file declares in `@module` against the name its path gives it.
messages.check.module-path-mismatch.why: A declared name that no `require` can reach is documentation of a module that does not exist; it is usually what a move or a rename left behind.
messages.check.orphaned-class-alias.compares: Every declared `@class` and `@alias` against the type references in the tree.
messages.check.orphaned-class-alias.why: A type nothing refers to is usually what a refactoring left behind, and it keeps describing a shape no value has any more.
messages.check.param-name-mismatch.compares: The name of each `@param` line against the parameter at the same position of the signature.
messages.check.param-name-mismatch.why: The usual cause is a parameter renamed in the code and not in the comment; the documentation then describes an argument that is not there.
messages.check.placeholder-readme-link.compares: Every link target in a README against the `${VAR}` placeholder form.
messages.check.placeholder-readme-link.why: No Markdown viewer expands a placeholder, so such a link works in nobody's browser, whatever the variable is set to.
messages.check.require-cycle.compares: The require edges of the tree against a loop among them.
messages.check.require-cycle.why: Modules that require each other load in an order nobody chose, and one of them sees the other half-built.
messages.check.require-not-declared.compares: Every require of a name under this project's own prefix against the modules the tree declares.
messages.check.require-not-declared.why: Such a require can only fail at run time: the name belongs to this tree and no file answers to it.
messages.check.sibling-reference-missing.compares: References into a sibling repository against that repository's checkout.
messages.check.sibling-reference-missing.why: A path into another repository breaks without a trace when that repository moves the file; nothing in this tree changes when it happens.
messages.check.tag-file-unavailable.compares: Every configured `tag_files` entry against a readable `module_map.json` at that place.
messages.check.tag-file-unavailable.why: Without the other project's map the requires into it were not checked at all, and a check that did not run must not read as one that passed.
messages.check.tag-require-missing.compares: The requires into another mapped project (`tag_files`) against the modules that project's own map declares.
messages.check.tag-require-missing.why: A require of a module the other project no longer has fails at run time, in a file this tree's own checks would call clean.
messages.check.test-references-missing.compares: The module members a spec file reaches for against what the module really has.
messages.check.test-references-missing.why: A spec that calls a function which is gone fails late, or never runs that part at all; either way it no longer tests what its name says.
messages.check.tools-spec-invalid.compares: Each entry of the tools manifest against the shape the manifest must have.
messages.check.tools-spec-invalid.why: An entry that does not parse is left out of the Tools panel and of every installer that reads the manifest, without anyone being told.
messages.check.type-vs-class.compares: A local annotated with `---@type` against the fields assigned to it after its literal.
messages.check.type-vs-class.why: LuaLS reports exactly this shape as injected or missing fields; `---@class` is the annotation that says what the code does.
messages.check.undocumented-param.compares: The number of parameters in a signature against the number of `@param` lines above it.
messages.check.undocumented-param.why: A documented function with fewer `@param` lines than parameters documents only part of its own call.
messages.check.unreferenced-module.compares: Every module against the requires of all other files in the tree.
messages.check.unreferenced-module.why: A module nothing requires is either an entry point or dead; the map cannot tell which, so it says that the question is open.
messages.check.unused-require.compares: Every `local x = require(...)` against the uses of `x` in the same file.
messages.check.unused-require.why: A require nobody uses still loads the module, costs startup time and draws a dependency edge in the map that is not real.

Same consequence as a missing directory: fn.tested stays false everywhere,

Not an error: a tree with no tests is a valid tree.

an untested repository rather than a misconfigured path.

messages.page.compare.clear.label: Clear all
messages.page.compare.clear.title: Drop every mark
messages.page.explain.atool.annotations: Which annotation tags this tree actually uses, counted per function. Generated, so unlike a hand-written inventory it cannot go stale.
messages.page.explain.atool.api: Every function this tree publishes, with its documentation state and how many other modules here call it — the question asked every time a module is extracted into its own plugin.
messages.page.explain.atool.bindings: Keymaps, user commands and autocommands registered in this tree. The `vim.*` APIs are recognised unconditionally; a config binding through its own wrapper needs `opts.bindings.wrappers` to declare it.
messages.page.explain.atool.checklist: Hand-verified facts, each cited to the file it was read off. The ledger is baked into this page; the changed-since-verified verdict needs git, so it fills in under `:DocMap serve`.
messages.page.explain.atool.complexity: Cyclomatic complexity per function, counted over its own subtree including nested closures. A ranking of where the branching is, not a threshold anything fails.
messages.page.explain.atool.decorators: Which decorators a Python tree uses, how often, and on which functions. Only Python files are checked for this.
messages.page.explain.atool.deps: Fan-in and fan-out per module: how many modules it requires, and how many require it. The second number is the one that decides how expensive a rename is.
messages.page.explain.atool.doc: Which functions carry a summary and fully documented parameters, per module, worst first. `@internal` functions are excluded — this is a question about the published surface, not about helpers.
messages.page.explain.atool.docs: Every Markdown file in the tree and how often the rest of the documentation points at it — which pages are load-bearing, and which nothing links to.
messages.page.explain.atool.duplicates: Functions whose parse-tree *shape* is identical, ignoring names and literals — the one kind of drift the require graph cannot see, since two modules that each grew their own `read(path)` do not require each other.
messages.page.explain.atool.endpoints: HTTP routes registered in the source, Express/Fastify/Koa-shaped. An ecosystem convention rather than a language feature, so a tree without one is empty here and that is a real answer.
messages.page.explain.atool.hooks: Functions named like a React hook (`^use[A-Z]`, the convention eslint-plugin-react-hooks itself relies on). Only JavaScript, TypeScript and TSX files are checked for this.
messages.page.explain.atool.lazy: The Plugins question inverted: which plugins load on each event, filetype, command and key, and which are paid for at startup regardless. Answers what typing a command actually costs, and why something is not loaded yet.
messages.page.explain.atool.loaded: A loaded-versus-declared comparison from a saved runtime-analysis snapshot. Needs `:DocMap serve` and a named snapshot — the difference is a property of one live session, never of a live aggregate.
messages.page.explain.atool.plugins: Every lazy.nvim-shaped plugin spec in the tree. Matters when this is pointed at a Neovim *config* rather than a plugin, where most files are specs with no function in them and are invisible to every other panel.
messages.page.explain.atool.rust: Which types implement which traits, and where `unsafe` lives: `unsafe fn` and functions holding `unsafe` blocks. Only Rust files are checked for this.
messages.page.explain.atool.startup: Where startup time went, as a flamegraph: width is total time, depth is require nesting. Measured by runtime-analysis.nvim and written by `:RATelemetry flamegraph`, then baked into this page — unlike Telemetry and Loaded it needs no `:DocMap serve`, because startup happens once per session rather than accumulating.
messages.page.explain.atool.telemetry: Call counts collected by runtime-analysis.nvim inside a real Neovim session, joined onto this map. Needs `:DocMap serve`: counts change between runs, so they are never baked into the committed page.
messages.page.explain.atool.test: Which functions a test suite mentions by name, per module, worst first. A floor rather than a verdict: a name found under the tests directory counts, and a function exercised only indirectly does not.
messages.page.explain.atool.tools: The CLI tools this repository declares it wants, from its own `docs/install.json`. Declared only — a static page has no host to ask whether any of them is installed here.
messages.page.explain.feat.theme: One feature file of this repository. The first is what the project exists for, the second the overview, the rest one theme each.
messages.page.explain.hier.entry: The module the rings are counted from. The list holds the roots of the require graph (modules that require something and that nothing requires) with how many modules each reaches. Any module can be the entry: click its box twice, or search for it.
messages.page.explain.hier.shape: Compares the map of a commit with this one, or the maps of two commits, and marks the difference on the diagram: nodes that were added, places nodes were removed from, requires gained and lost. Nothing moves; what did not change is dimmed. Needs a server that can read git.
messages.page.explain.hier.tint: Tints the Modules boxes by one measure of everything below each box: the share of functions that are documented or tested, or how many FIX or TODO/HACK/PERF markers there are per 1,000 lines. A stronger tint means look here first. The value is printed on each box and the legend names the steps.
messages.page.explain.sub.features.all: The index of every feature file, above the ones promoted to a tab of their own.
messages.page.explain.sub.functions: Every documented function in the map, alphabetically, with its signature and where it lives.
messages.page.explain.sub.modules: Every module and namespace, alphabetically. The same set the tree shows, without the nesting.
messages.page.explain.sub.tree: The module tree as the scan walked it, with each node's own detail beside it. The default place to start reading a repository you do not know.
messages.page.explain.tab.analysis: Aggregate numbers over the whole tree: how much is tested, how much is documented, where dependencies concentrate. A palette of tools sharing one panel, not a single report.
messages.page.explain.tab.compare: Two or more modules side by side, on the same rows, so a difference is a difference in a column rather than something to remember between scrolls.
messages.page.explain.tab.features: This repository's own `docs/FEATURES/` files, read as an index — name, summary and metadata. Never the prose that follows them, which stays in the file it was written in.
messages.page.explain.tab.findings: Where the drift checks report. Each row is one check disagreeing with the code — a doc reference to something that no longer exists, an example that does not parse, a binding declared twice. The same list that fails CI and lands on GitHub as SARIF. Its count stays in the header rather than moving in here, because a number behind a click is a number nobody reads.
messages.page.explain.tab.hierarchy: The dependency graph, drawn from one module outward. Boxes are modules and namespaces, arrows are requires and calls; the slider decides how far from the centre it reaches. Hovering a box lights it and its neighbours; the first click holds that, so you can read it and follow the edges without the pointer. Click the same box again to root the graph there — or double-click, which is the same two clicks at once. Escape, a click on empty space, or a click on another box lets go. The path above the graph shows where you are, every level a way back. The *Classic clicks* pill decides what that second click does: root here, or open in the Tree. The one view that exports as an SVG.
messages.page.explain.tab.history: This repository's git history, and what each commit did to the map. Computed on demand from git, so it needs a host that can run it — a map opened as a file says so instead of guessing.
messages.page.explain.tab.index: Flat lists of everything the map found, for when you know the name and not the place. Three ways of listing the same repository — as a tree, as functions, as modules.
messages.page.explain.tab.notes: Everything the authors left behind. Annotations on functions (`---@todo`, `---@bug`) and marker comments in the source (`-- TODO:`, `// FIXME:`) — two lists, because one is attached to a signature and the other to a line.
messages.page.explain.tab.quicks: The verdicts: what is notable about this tree stated in sentences, good and bad, each with the count it is based on. Computed by the engine, not by this page.
messages.page.explain.view.calls: Function-level callers and callees, resolved from real call sites rather than guessed. A weak match is drawn dimmed rather than hidden — see the Findings tab for what could not be resolved.
messages.page.explain.view.coupling: Every module as a dot: how many modules it requires across, how many require it up. The corners have names (hubs, tangles, pass-throughs, leaves) and say what would be expensive to change.
messages.page.explain.view.deps: The require graph: an arrow means this module requires that one. `+ external` adds the modules outside this map, each box naming the functions actually called through it.
messages.page.explain.view.inheritance: Only `@class Child : Parent` edges, drawn apart from Types because inheritance is a different claim than collaboration and reading both in one picture hides which is which.
messages.page.explain.view.layers: The tree in the bands its layering rules imply: a layer that may not require another sits below it. A require that breaks a rule is a red arrow, which is the layer-violation finding as a picture. Needs layers in .docmap.json.
messages.page.explain.view.modulecalls: The same call graph collapsed module to module, with each edge weighted by how many calls it carries. Answers which modules lean on each other, where Calls answers which functions do.
messages.page.explain.view.modules: The directory hierarchy itself — every module and namespace, nested the way the tree is. The one view with no direction, because containment has none; the slider hides the top N levels instead.
messages.page.explain.view.rings: Every module on the ring of its shortest require chain from the entry: how deep the tree is and what is reachable at all. What the entry does not reach sits in a last, dashed ring, where the unreferenced-module findings are marked. Point at a box to see its chain.
messages.page.explain.view.routes: File-based routing as a tree: the Next.js app and pages directories, a box per segment, with the URL where a page or a handler makes it a route. Dynamic segments, route groups and slots are named as written. Routes registered by a call are in Analysis, under Endpoints.
messages.page.explain.view.tree: The same directory hierarchy as Modules, as a list you fold: a level is a column of rows instead of a row of boxes, so a level with two hundred modules stays readable. The filter keeps every match and the path to it.
messages.page.explain.view.treemap: Everything under the center as nested areas, sized by lines of code (or functions): where the weight of a wide level sits, at a glance. Click to zoom in.
messages.page.explain.view.types: How `@class` and `@alias` declarations reference each other through their fields. Needs LuaLS enrichment (`:DocMap full`) — without it this is empty rather than wrong.

messages.report.quicks.avg-fn-lines.bad: Your functions run long on average

report.quicks.avg-fn-lines.basis.one: Mean source span (`line` to `line_end`) across {count} function. A long mean is a smell, not a defect — a table-driven dispatcher is legitimately long.
report.quicks.avg-fn-lines.basis.other: Mean source span (`line` to `line_end`) across {count} functions. A long mean is a smell, not a defect — a table-driven dispatcher is legitimately long.

messages.report.quicks.avg-fn-lines.good: Your functions are short on average
messages.report.quicks.complexity.bad: A lot of functions sit above complexity {threshold}

report.quicks.complexity.basis.one: Cyclomatic complexity (McCabe), counted over each function's own subtree including nested closures. {count} function above the line.
report.quicks.complexity.basis.other: Cyclomatic complexity (McCabe), counted over each function's own subtree including nested closures. {count} functions above the line.

messages.report.quicks.complexity.good: Nearly every function stays under complexity {threshold}
messages.report.quicks.deprecated.bad: Deprecated functions are still in the tree
messages.report.quicks.deprecated.basis: Counts functions carrying `@deprecated`. Whether that is overdue depends on a deprecation window this map knows nothing about.
messages.report.quicks.doc-coverage.bad: Most of your published API is undocumented
messages.report.quicks.doc-coverage.basis: A function counts as documented when it has a summary and every parameter is annotated correctly. `@internal` functions are excluded.
messages.report.quicks.doc-coverage.good: Your published API is well documented
messages.report.quicks.docs-mentions.bad: Your prose docs mention only a fraction of the tree

report.quicks.docs-mentions.basis.one: Counts modules referenced from a code span in one of the {count} scanned `.md` file.
report.quicks.docs-mentions.basis.other: Counts modules referenced from a code span in one of the {count} scanned `.md` files.

messages.report.quicks.docs-mentions.good: Your prose docs actually reach most of the tree
messages.report.quicks.drift-errors.bad: The map has drifted from the tree
messages.report.quicks.drift-errors.basis: Error-severity findings from the drift checks — the same set `:DocMap check` fails a pre-commit hook on.
messages.report.quicks.drift-errors.good: The map is in sync with the tree
messages.report.quicks.drift-warnings.bad: The drift checks raised a pile of warnings
messages.report.quicks.drift-warnings.basis: Warn-severity findings. These never fail `:DocMap check`.
messages.report.quicks.drift-warnings.good: Nothing in the tree raised a warning
messages.report.quicks.duplicates.bad: Several functions are structural copies of each other

report.quicks.duplicates.basis.one: Groups functions by a hash of their parse-tree node types, so a renamed copy still matches. {count} function across those groups. Sharing a shape is not automatically wrong — two folds over the same shape are legitimate.
report.quicks.duplicates.basis.other: Groups functions by a hash of their parse-tree node types, so a renamed copy still matches. {count} functions across those groups. Sharing a shape is not automatically wrong — two folds over the same shape are legitimate.

messages.report.quicks.duplicates.good: No two functions share a structure
messages.report.quicks.examples.bad: Almost nothing in your published API shows how to call it
messages.report.quicks.examples.good: A good share of your published API carries a usage example
messages.report.quicks.module-summary.bad: Many files have no description at the top
messages.report.quicks.module-summary.basis: Counts a non-empty summary in the file's leading doc-comment block. Namespace directories are excluded — they have no file to hold one.
messages.report.quicks.module-summary.good: Nearly every file opens with a description
messages.report.quicks.recorded-defects.bad: There are defects marked in the source and still there
messages.report.quicks.recorded-defects.basis: Counts `FIX`/`FIXME`/`BUG`/`FIXIT`/`ISSUE` comment markers. This is the author's own claim about their code, not a finding of this tool's -- nothing here was verified, and nothing fails `:DocMap check` because of it.
messages.report.quicks.recorded-defects.good: No line is marked as currently broken
messages.report.quicks.test-coverage.bad: Most of your published API is never named in a spec
messages.report.quicks.test-coverage.basis: Auto-derived and coarse: a function counts as tested when its bare name appears somewhere under `tests_dir`. That means 'not found by name', not 'definitely untested' — and a name matched there was not necessarily executed.
messages.report.quicks.test-coverage.good: Most of your published API is named in a spec
messages.report.quicks.todos.bad: There is a backlog of `@todo`/`@bug` annotations
messages.report.quicks.todos.basis: Counts `@todo` and `@bug` entries on functions. Written-down work is better than undocumented work — a high number here is a reading, not an accusation.
